extracted.intended_audience: historians of mathematics, classical geometers, and advanced students studying ancient Greek geometry
extracted.subtask_description: Interpretation and evaluation of Hippocrates's quadratures of lunes and the related ancient geometrical propositions, including textual-criticism issues about Eudemus and Simplicius. The page assesses mathematical conditions for squaring lunes and the prerequisite theorems and constructions assumed by ancient authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similar segments as ratios of squares on their bases
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposition that similar segments of circles have the same ratio to one another as the squares on their bases have.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eudemus (as quoted) states this as a first useful theorem; it is proved by first showing that the squares on the diameters have the same ratio as the circles, and then transferring that ratio to segments (via similar sectors/triangles). The passage is debated over whether 'segments' may mean 'sectors' in places; the author discusses implications for the chain of reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circles are to one another as the squares on their diameters
rubrics_metrics.description: "Circles are to one another as the squares on their diameters" (Euclid XII.2) — used as a foundational proposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eudemus is reported to have used this proposition as the basis for proving the ratio statement about similar segments. The book notes Euclid's proof uses exhaustion and Archimedean lemmas, and queries how Hippocrates could have proved it without similar methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similar segments contain equal angles
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim (in the extract) that similar segments contain equal angles (i.e., segments are similar when they contain equal angles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The sentence's provenance is disputed (Eudemus vs Simplicius). If accepted as Eudemian, it underpins constructions and inferences; if an interpolation, it may have been inserted to relate Hippocrates' view to Euclid's definition. The text examines semantic issues over whether 'segments' could mean 'sectors' and whether the definition was already Euclidean in Hippocrates's time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textual attribution criteria (three 'ifs' for Rudio's interpretation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed acceptance of Rudio's interpretation requires three conditions: (1) the passage is genuinely Eudemian, (2) the term 'segments' (r/hfjta) can validly be used in different senses in successive sentences without explanation, (3) omission of intermediate logical steps can be ascribed to Eudemus's 'summary' style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author evaluates each of the three conditions and ultimately finds the second (shifting senses without notice) implausible, using canons of literary criticism. These 'ifs' are presented as criteria to judge the plausibility of a reconstruction of ancient reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of sectors to justify ratio-transfer to segments
rubrics_metrics.description: Similar sectors, having equal angles, are to one another as the whole circles to which they belong; therefore they are as the squares on the radii, and differences between sectors and corresponding triangles (i.e., segments) inherit the same ratio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the chain of geometric argument (attributed to the Rudio reconstruction) that would allow proving the proposition about segments via sectors and triangles, presupposing knowledge of certain Euclidean results (and possibly Theon's addition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prerequisite theorems and constructions assumed
rubrics_metrics.description: Hippocrates' arguments assume several Euclidean-type theorems and constructions: (a) similar segments contain equal angles (Eucl. III.20-22), (b) construction of a segment similar on a given straight line (Eucl. III.33), (c) theorems III.26-29 and III.31 about angles in semicircles and segments, (d) circumscribing a circle about a triangle (Eucl. IV.5), (e) side of a regular hexagon equals the radius (Eucl. IV.15).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author lists these as hypothesized background knowledge required for Hippocrates' quadrature constructions and uses them to argue what methods Hippocrates must have known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessary algebraic/trigonometric condition for a lune to be squareable
rubrics_metrics.description: In order that the lune may be squareable, we must have, in the first place, r^2 θ = r'^2 θ'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using trigonometric reduction of areas (sectors minus triangles), the area condition emerges; together with the chord relation r sin θ = r' sin θ' (equation (1) in text) these lead to a functional equation in sines that determines which lunes are squareable by 'plane' methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equation reducing to solvable algebraic cases (m parameter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume θ = m θ'; then r' = sqrt(m) r and the trigonometric relation reduces to sin(m θ') = sqrt(m) sin θ'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes this reduces to a quadratic equation only for certain values of m (the text lists specific small values and states Hippocrates' solutions correspond to the first three). Later commentators found more solvable cases; historically the reducibility to low-degree algebraic equations controls which lunes admit classical squaring constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical vs theoretical construction methods for solving 'vergings' problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems of finding a straight line EF of specified square-length so that a line produced 'verges' towards a point (a geometric placement leading to a quadratic condition) can be solved either theoretically (Euclidean/Pythagorean method, II.6) or by a mechanical ruler-marking method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author discusses plausibility: Hippocrates could have solved such quadratic-placement problems by theoretical Pythagorean constructions or by practical/mechanical methods (marking and moving a ruler). This distinction is used as a criterion when assessing what Hippocrates likely did in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of area-addition/subtraction arguments to equate lunes and rectilineal figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Technique: express sectors/segments as sums and differences of segments/triangles, add or subtract common parts (e.g., segments bounded by straight lines), to show a lune equals a triangle or a rectilineal figure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the operative method in Hippocrates' quadratures as reported: circumscribe segments similar to others, compare sums of segment areas via diameter/side-square relations, then add/subtract shared areas so that a lune becomes equal to a polygonal (squarable) figure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textual-criticism criterion: archaic phrasing is not definitive evidence of verbatim quotation
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence of older, longer archaic locutions in a passage does not safely indicate that the passage is a verbatim quotation from an earlier author (e.g., Eudemus quoting Hippocrates).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author warns against assuming that archaic expression equals direct quotation, noting even Aristotle uses both archaic and later forms, and that archaisms survive in later authors; thus textual attribution should use multiple criteria, not solely archaic phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive possibilities for Aristotle's charge of fallacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Simplicius lists three hypotheses to interpret Aristotle's remark that Hippocrates 'squared the circle' fallaciously: (1) Aristotle meant squaring the circle by means of lunes, (2) the charge refers to other proofs (not Hippocrates'), (3) Aristotle intended criticism of squaring the circle plus a lune (i.e., the sum), not the circle alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These three interpretive options are presented as alternate readings; evaluating which holds requires checking what Hippocrates actually proved and whether his language could have been construed as claiming the circle alone was squared.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical plausibility criterion about claimed discovery vs. rhetorical emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: When ancient authors use language that might mislead (e.g., suggesting a more successful result than actually achieved), consider whether the mathematician intentionally exaggerated or simply phrased results in the most favourable light without self-deception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author discusses whether Hippocrates might have misstated or overstated his achievements and concludes it is unlikely he deceived himself or deliberately tried to mislead experts; rather, he likely sought to present discoveries favourably. This is a criterion when judging authorial intent from phrasing.
